ety.text: An Arabised rendition of ख़ुदा हाफ़िज़ (xudā hāfiz), from Classical Persian خدا حافظ (xudā hāfiz, “May the Lord be your protector”); in which the Classical Persian خُدَا (xudā, “god”) is replaced by the Arabic اللّٰه (allāh, “God; Allah”). First attested in c. 19th century, but only came into common usage in Pakistan in the 1980s, and thus in India only after the beginning of the 21st century as a learned borrowing from Urdu اللہ حافِظ (allāh hāfiz). Cognate with Bengali আল্লাহ হাফেজ (allah haphej).

Borrowed from Classical Persian باره, or from बार (bār) + -आ (-ā).

Often derived from Sanskrit वीजन (vījana, “fanning; fan”) or व्यजन (vyajana, “fan”), but the retention of -j- indicates derivation from a Middle Indo-Aryan verb with vijj- (e.g., Prakrit 𑀯𑀺𑀚𑁆𑀚𑀺𑀚𑁆𑀚𑀇 (vijjijjaï, “is fanned”), from Sanskrit वीज्यते (vījyate)) and possible adaptation to forms like वीजन (vījana). Compare Bengali বিউনি (biuni), from Sanskrit वीजन (vījana), and Eastern Hindi बेना (benā), from Sanskrit व्यजन (vyajana), both of which have lost the -j- sound. Cognate with Gujarati વીજણો (vījṇo), Marathi विजणा (vij̈ṇā), Bengali বিজনি, বিজনী (bijoni).
By surface analysis, बीज (bīj, “seed”) + -ना (-nā, verbal suffix).
